On the autumn equinox, when the swallows gathered along the eastern wire and the orchard turned the color of old copper, a door appeared behind the barn. It had no hinges, no frame, and no wall around it, only a narrow slab of dark wood with a brass knob and a dusty square window. Sela found it after she went to collect the last basket of apples. The grass beneath it was unworn. The air smelled of rain that had not yet fallen. Evening lay across the hills, and from the valley far below, a lonely train whistle sounded twice.

Her grandfather had told her about the door, though he never mentioned seeing it himself. He said her father had found it on this same night, thirty years earlier. He had stepped through to search for their missing dog, Pepper, and returned an hour later with flour on his sleeves and no recognition in his eyes. He still spoke kindly to Sela, but he spoke to her the way a stranger might speak to a child waiting for a lost parent. Every autumn afterward, he polished the brass knob as if some fragment of it had followed him back home.

Sela knew the stories her family had built around that vanished hour. Her father had crossed a field, found the dog waiting beside a lake, and come home unable to remember either of them. But the lake was dry now, and Pepper had never existed. Only the door insisted otherwise. Sela rested her palm against the wood. It was warm. Through the dusty glass she saw a street illuminated by a pale morning sun, though outside the orchard evening had only just begun. Her father had warned her never to open doors that disagreed with the sky, even in daylight.

She turned the knob. The door swung inward without a creak, opening not onto a field but onto a city asleep beneath clear morning light. Buildings leaned together along narrow streets. Their windows shone blue and gold. Bread cooled on a bakery counter. A black cat watched her from a rain barrel, then vanished when she approached. Nothing moved except a curtain lifting on an upstairs window, though Sela could hear footsteps, distant bells, and a great many people breathing in their sleep. The air tasted of snow, lamp oil, and oranges peeled for a festival that had not happened.

The bakery bell chimed. A young man emerged from the back room wiping his hands on a floury apron. He had her father's square jaw, his brown hair, and a small scar above his left eyebrow. Sela could not speak. He looked at her as if she were a stranger he had expected to meet, then bent and rearranged the loaves until every loaf faced the same direction. “You came through before,” he said. “Or you will. It is difficult to remember the order here.” He smiled at her with the cautious tenderness reserved for beautiful news that no one must speak.

“This is where unfinished days go,” her father said, though she had not asked. “Every tomorrow begins here. A little courage. A little luck. The kindness of a stranger. When they are ready, they travel forward and become real.” Sela looked at him. “Then why are you still here?” He touched the counter, leaving a bright print in the flour. “Because someone must finish the loaf I started. Besides, I no longer remember how to want a world beyond this one.” Outside, the sleeping city seemed less beautiful, and every blue window seemed to conceal a terrible hunger beneath it.

He took her outside. They passed a theater where an actor rehearsed the same farewell beneath a blood red moon. They passed gardens filled with flowers that had no names, their petals humming with the plans of pollinators. Near the river, a little girl sat beneath a silver umbrella, watching reflections move beneath the bridge. “People spend whole lives here,” the girl said. “They call it waiting. They call it wisdom. Mostly, they are too frightened to be bored.” She offered Sela half a pear. It tasted exactly like pears remembered from childhood. Her father watched her as though remembering a puzzling question.

“What happened to the hour you lost?” Sela asked. Her father was quiet for a long time. “It bought your grandmother a good winter,” he finally said. “The fever that was coming never arrived. Your grandfather planted an orchard. You were born. No one remembers an illness, so no one knows what debt was paid.” Sela looked at the sleeping houses. “Was it worth it? You never remembered us.” “I remembered love,” he said. “Love is a stubborn thing. It survives its own explanation.” His voice was gentle, and the floury light made him seem familiar and strangely young again.

Before they returned to the bakery, he showed her a clock with no hands and a jar holding one bright, slow turning spark. “This is a minute I saved,” he said. “Take it home. Give it to whoever needs it.” Sela closed her fingers around the jar. “Come with me.” He shook his head. “The door permits one person, and besides, I am not your lost father. I am what he became when he chose a stranger’s tomorrow.” Still, she took his hand. For a moment he remembered her name. Then he let go, and morning faded gently around her.

She stepped through holding the borrowed minute, and the orchard received her in the hush that had greeted her before. Her grandfather sat beneath the apple tree, peeling a spiral of skin. He looked up. She told him everything, though he believed none of it. Still, when she placed the jar in his hands, his eyes filled with tears. The spark brightened, then sank into his palm. That spring, he remembered her father’s laugh. Every equinox afterward, the door returned, but Sela never entered. She had learned that love was not a key. It was a home carried within us.
